Abstract 
35 
Lyme disease , caused by an infection with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, is the most common 
36 
vector-borne disease in North America.  B. burgdorferi strains harbor extensive genomic and 
37 
proteomic variability and further comparison is key to understanding the spirochetes infectivity and 
38 
biological impacts of identified sequence variants.  To achieve this goal, both transcript and mass 
39 
spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics was applied to assemble peptide datasets of laboratory 
40 
strains B31, MM1, B31-ML23, infective isolates B31-5A4, B31-A3, and 297, and other public 
41 
datasets, 
to 
provide 
a 
publicly 
available 
Borrelia 
PeptideAtlas 
42 
(http://www.peptideatlas.org/builds/borrelia/). Included is information on total proteome, 
43 
secretome, and membrane proteome of these B. burgdorferi strains.  Proteomic data collected from 
44 
35 different experiment datasets, with a total of 855 mass spectrometry runs, identified 76,936 
45 
distinct peptides at a 0.1% peptide false-discovery-rate, which map to 1,221 canonical proteins (924 
46 
core canonical and 297 noncore canonical) and covers 86% of the total base B31 proteome.  The 
47 
diverse proteomic information from multiple isolates with credible data presented by the Borrelia 
48

PeptideAtlas can be useful to pinpoint potential protein targets which are common to infective 
49 
isolates and may be key in the infection process.

Background & Summary 
53 
The spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi is the causative agent of Lyme disease, the main vector-borne 
54 
infection in North America, with over 476,000 cases per year between 2010 and 2018 [1, 2].  B. 
55 
burgdorferi is transmitted to humans through the bite of infected nymphal or adult blacklegged 
56 
ticks, and the untreated infection may cause a multisystem disorder characterized by early and later 
57 
stage signs and symptoms [3, 4].  The early stage symptoms happen within the first 30 days after 
58 
the tick bite and may include, among others, fever, joint aches and swollen lymph nodes, and rash 
59 
(erythema migrans) [3].  When symptoms persist for months after the tick bite, later symptoms 
60 
could be manifested: facial palsy, arthritis with severe joint pain and swelling, severe headaches, 
61 
and inflammation of the brain [3].  Treatment is done with the use of antibiotics, and most cases of 
62 
Lyme disease can be cured within 2 to 4 weeks [5], even though patients may continue to present 
63 
symptoms for more than 6 months after the treatment ends, condition called Post-Treatment Lyme 
64 
Disease Syndrome (PTLDS) [6].  Therefore, an early and correct diagnosis of Lyme disease is key to 
65 
initiate the treatment of infection at its early stages and prevent extreme symptoms.  Currently 
66 
available tests, including the current CDC-recommended 2-tiered testing protocol, are designed to 
67 
detect antibodies against B. burgdorferi in patient blood, which takes several weeks to be produced 
68 
and can result in a false negative diagnosis [7].  Therefore, the development of alternative diagnostic 
69 
methodologies, such as next-generation serologic assays [7], which include recombinant proteins 
70 
and synthetic peptides targeting important factors in the B. burgdorferi infection, survival and 
71 
proliferation mechanisms are needed.   
72 
Borrelia burgdorferi is an atypical Gram-negative bacteria due to lack of LPS in its cell wall and the 
73 
presence of immuno-reactive glycolipids, a peptidoglycan layer, and lipoproteins in the outer 
74 
membrane [8-11] (Figure 1).  These lipoproteins play a key role in the infectivity and proliferation 
75 
of the spirochete in ticks and in mammal hosts [12], and are mostly encoded by the spirochete linear 
76 
and circular plasmids, besides the single chromosome harbored [13].  Specifically, the B. burgdorferi 
77 
B31 genome sequence revealed the presence of one linear chromosome with 843 genes, and 21 
78 
plasmids (12 linear and 9 circular) with 670 genes and 167 pseudogenes [9, 14].  Out of a total of 
79 
1,513 genes, 1,291 are predicted as unique protein-coding genes [14].  B31 is the most commonly 
80 
studied B. burgdorferi non-infective laboratory isolate, but an increasing number of infective 
81 
genotypes have been isolated in North America and around the world, which are isolated from 
82 
infected ticks or Lyme patients and display different pathogenic and infective patterns [15].  The 
83 
genetic variability of subtypes of B. burgdorferi isolates – e.g., varying number of plasmids encoding 
84 
for infection-related lipoproteins – may ultimately lead to diverse (i) severity of Lyme symptoms 
85 
and (ii) spirochetal response to the antibiotic treatment [15].  Hence a proteogenomic approach 
86 
combining genome sequencing data with transcriptomic and proteomic data from different isolates 
87

is a robust strategy to unveil the Borrelia pathogenicity and begin to develop new strategies for 
88 
more efficient diagnosis and treatment of Lyme disease.   
89 
Although numerous proteomic reports exist for B. burgdorferi isolates [16-23], no information is 
90 
available as a searchable compendium of public data, and users have to resort to obtaining raw 
91 
information files and search any, or all, of these data individually.  In this study, we include in-house 
92 
acquired mass spectrometry (MS) and publicly available data to perform a comprehensive 
93 
proteome analysis of 6 different laboratory B. burgdorferi isolates: two commercially available 
94 
isolates B31 [24] and MM1 [25, 26], the genotype B31-ML23 [27], and 3 infective isolates 297 [28], 
95 
B31-A3 [18], and B31-5A4 [29].  These datasets include information on the total proteome, 
96 
secretome, and membrane proteome of the Borrelia isolates (Figure 1a&b).  The uniform analysis 
97 
of the total 855 MS runs through the Trans-Proteomic Pipeline (TPP) (Figure 1c) allowed the

99

100 
level FDR less than 1% covering 86% of the total B31 proteome coverage.  Additionally, for the 
101 
comparison of protein abundance levels with mRNA levels, we performed transcriptomic analysis 
102 
of isolates B31, 5A4-B31, and MM1.  The complex and detailed proteomic results achieved here 
103 
were gathered in a public repository called Borrelia PeptideAtlas, with interface made available at 
104 
http://www.peptideatlas.org/builds/borrelia/.  PeptideAtlas is a unique public community resource 
105 
which contains large scale assembly of mass spectrometry data uniformly processed through the 
106 
TPP [30, 31].  This repository has data from a wide range of samples, e.g., including human, 
107 
Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Drosophila melanogaster and Candida albicans [32-36] among others.  
108 
The Borrelia PeptideAtlas allows the assessment of protein content of B. burgdorferi isolates and 
109 
compare detectable protein sequences.  The continuous update of this repository with expandable 
110 
data sources for many other B. burgdorferi isolates, including clinically relevant isolates, will enable 
111 
the investigation of the dynamic proteome of this spirochete through its infection stages and their 
112 
vastly different environments.  The diverse proteomic information from multiple infective isolates 
113 
with credible data presented by the Borrelia PeptideAtlas can be useful to understand the protein 
114 
complement of each isolate and assist in pinpointing potential protein targets which are common 
115 
to infective isolates and may be key in the infection process.  The Borrelia PeptideAtlas is readily 
116 
available as an important resource for the Lyme disease research community.

Methods 
127 
B. burgdorferi isolates and spirochete culture 
128 
For the in-house performed experiments, 2 common commercially available laboratory isolates of 
129 
B. burgdorferi [B31 (ATCC 35210) [24], MM1 (ATCC 51990) [25, 26]], and the infective isolate B31-
130 
5A4 (a clonal isolate of 5A4 that has been passaged through rodents to maintain infectivity) [29] 
131 
were cultured in BSK-H complete media with 10% rabbit serum, at 34 °C in 5.0% CO2 incubator.  B31-
132 
5A4 was cultured at a low passage to minimize loss of endogenous plasmids.  The spirochetes were 
133 
harvested and collected at mid-log phase (3 to 5 × 107) or stationary phase (3 to 5 × 108) for 
134 
proteomic analysis.  For secretome analysis, mid-log phase cells were harvested, washed and 
135 
transferred to serum-free media, i.e., BSK-H media without rabbit serum grown for 24 h at 34 °C in 
136 
5.0% CO2 incubator.  The culture was centrifuged at 3,000 rpm for 1 h and collected both the media 
137 
and the bacteria were collected.  The media was used for secretome analysis and bacteria were 
138 
used for stress proteome analysis.   
139 
Total proteome extraction 
140 
B. burgdorferi pellets collected from log phase, stationary phase and stressed bacteria (grown in 
141 
serum-free media for 24 h) were washed with PBS buffer (pH 7.4) four times to remove the media 
142 
and centrifuged at 300 × g for 3 min at each wash.  The bacterial pellets were dispersed in lysis 
143 
buffer of 8 M urea in 100 mM ammonium bicarbonate and protease inhibitor cocktail (CoMplete, 
144 
(Roche)).  The bacterial cell lysis was performed using freeze-thaw cycle followed by sonication (30 
145 
s pulse, 20% amplitude, 5 cycles).  Cell lysate was centrifuged at 25,000 rpm for 30 min and clear 
146 
supernatant was collected for total proteome analysis.  The protein samples were stored at - 80 °C 
147 
until used.   
148 
Secretome extraction 
149 
B. burgdorferi B31 culture at mid-log phase was washed with PBS buffer to remove the media and 
150 
allow transfer of the bacteria to serum free BSK media (BSK media without rabbit serum) for 24 hrs.  
151 
The bacteria were collected by centrifugation at 300 × g for 3 min, and the media was used for the 
152 
secretome analysis.  To the media, four volumes of chilled acetone were added and precipitated 
153 
the protein for 30 min at 4 °C.  Protein pellets were collected by centrifugation and washed with 
154 
acetone two more times.  Protein pellet was dissolved in lysis buffer (8 M urea in 100 mM 
155 
ammonium bicarbonate).   
156 
Membrane proteome analysis 
157 
B. burgdorferi B31 was cultured as above and harvested by centrifugation at 3,000 rpm for 60 min. 
158 
The bacterial pellets were washed with ice cold PBS buffer (pH 8.0) three times.  The bacterial pellets 
159

were resuspended in PBS buffer (pH 8.0) with final cell number of 108/mL of buffer.  10 mM Sulfo-
160 
NHS-SS-Biotin (Thermo-Fisher Scientific, USA) was prepared according to the manufacture’s guide.  
161 
The stock solution of Sulfo-NHS-SS-Biotin was added to the bacterial pellets and mixed via pipette.  
162 
The bacterial pellets were incubated at 4 °C for 60 min for the labeling reaction.  Each bacterial 
163 
pellet was centrifuged at 5,000 rpm for 20 min and supernatant was discarded.  Tris buffered saline 
164 
(TBS, pH 7.4) was added to the bacterial pellets and incubated at room temperature for 15 min and 
165 
centrifuged at 16,000 rpm for 10 min.  B. burgdorferi pellets were washed with PBS buffer (pH 7.4) 
166 
and dispersed in 100 mM Tris buffer (pH 8.0) containing the protease inhibitor cocktail.  The cell 
167 
lysis was performed using freeze-thaw cycles as described above.  The B. burgdorferi B31 lysate was 
168 
centrifuged at 25,000 rpm for 30 min and the supernatant was collected for soluble proteome 
169 
analysis.  The resultant protein pellet was washed with 100 mM Tris buffer (pH 8.0) and dissolved 
170 
in membrane dissolving buffer (8 M urea having protease inhibitor cocktail) and incubated at 4 °C

180 
In-solution digestion and high-pH fractionation 
181 
Isolates B31, MM1 and B31-5A4 protein samples (log phase, stationary phase, stressed bacteria, 
182 
and secretome) were digested with trypsin for proteomic analysis.  Briefly, 100 µg of protein from 
183 
each condition were reduced with 5 mM Tris (2-carboxyethyl) phosphine (TCEP) and alkylated with 
184 
iodoacetamide.  Proteomic-grade modified trypsin (Promega) was added at a 50:1 protein-to-
185 
enzyme ratio and incubated at 37 °C overnight.  Samples were fractionated using high-pH 
186 
fractionation, and the remaining samples were analyzed by LC-MS/MS directly.  In the first 
187 
experiment set trypsin digested peptides were reconstituted in 200 mM ammonium formate (pH 
188 
10) and fractionated on an Agilent 1200 Series HPLC system.  Peptides were loaded on ZORBAX SB-
189

C18 column (4.6 × 150 mm, 5 µm particle size) and fractionated using a linear gradient of 0-100% of 
190 
B (60% acetonitrile in 20 mM ammonium formate pH 10).  A total of 24 fractions were collected 
191 
over the elution profile and pooled to create 8 disparate fractions, each containing 3 of the original 
192 
24, separated by 7 fractions in between ,i.e. (1,9,17), (2,10,18), (3,11,19)  etc.  For B31, B31-5A4 and 
193 
MM1 protein samples tryptic peptides were fractionated on the Agilent 1200 Series Gradient HPLC 
194 
system with a flow rate of 100 µL/min of buffer A [0.1% (vol/vol) triethylammonium bicarbonate 
195 
(TEAB) in water] and 1%/min gradient of buffer B [60% (vol/vol) acetonitrile, 0.1% (vol/vol) TEAB in 
196 
water], with a Brownlee Aquapore RP-300 column (100 mm × 2.1 mm i.d. from Perkin-Elmer).  The 
197 
total 56 fractions were pooled to 14 final fractions through groupings of 3 disparate fractions to 
198 
cover the range.  These fractions were lyophilized and reconstituted in 0.1% formic acid and 2% 
199 
acetonitrile for LC-MS/MS analysis.   
200 
SDS-PAGE and in-gel digestion 
201 
The biotin labeled proteins eluted in 2 × SDS-PAGE sample buffers were mixed with reducing agent 
202 
and bromophenol blue (BPB) and resolved on 12% SDS-PAGE gel.  The gel was stained with 
203 
SimplyBlue Safe Stain (Invitrogen, Carlsbad, CA).  Each lane of the SDS-PAGE was cut into five bands 
204 
and processed for in-gel digestion.  In brief, the gel pieces were washed with 50 mM ammonium 
205 
bicarbonate (AmBic) and 2:1 ratio of acetonitrile:AmBic alternatively,three times for five min each 
206 
to remove the stain.  Gel bands were treated with DTT (56 °C for 1 h) and iodoacetamide (20 min in 
207 
the dark) for reducing and alkylating the cysteine residues.  Trypsin (500 ng/µL) along with sufficient 
208 
50 mM AmBic was added to each gel band and incubated at 37 °C overnight.  Peptide elution was 
209 
performed by adding 60% of acetonitrile in 0.1% TFA to the bands,vortexing for 10 min and collectint 
210 
the solution into a fresh tube.  The process was repeated two more times with acetonitrile gradient 
211 
70% and 80% in 0.1% TFA and pooled to the previous fraction.   
212 
Enrichment of phosphorylated peptides 
213 
For the enrichment of phosphorylated peptides of isolates B31-5A4 and MM1, tryptic peptides from 
214 
log phase pellets (~5 × 107 cells) were resuspended in 500 µL of loading buffer [80% acetonitrile, 5% 
215 
trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), 0.1 M glycolic acid], and incubated with 400 µg of MagReSyn Ti-IMAC HP 
216 
(Resyn Biosciences).  Beads were washed 3 times with 500 µL of 80% acetonitrile and 1% TFA, 3

220 
LC-MS/MS analysis 
221 
Q-Exactive HF 
222 
Borrelia burgdorferi samples, except B31-Biotin labeled samples, were analyzed either on an 
223 
EasynLC (Thermo Fisher Scientific) coupled with Q-Exactive HF mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher 
224 
Scientific).  The purified dried peptides were dissolved in loading buffer (0.1% formic acid (FA) in 
225 
water) and loaded on to the Acclaim PepMap 100 trap (2 cm long, 75 μm ID, C18 3 μm; Thermo 
226 
Fisher Scientific).  Analytical column (PICOCHIP: 105 cm, 1.9 µm, REPROSIL Pur C-18-AQ, 120 Å, New 
227 
Objective, USA) with a flow rate of 300 nL/min was used for the separation of the peptides with a 
228 
linear gradient of 5–35% buffer-B (90% acetonitrile in 0.1% FA) over 120 min.  The data acquisition 
229 
parameters include: mass range 375-1375 m/z, MS resolution of 30,000 (at m/z 200), MS/MS 
230 
resolution of 15,000 (at m/z 200), full scan target at 3 × 106, 40 top intense peaks with charge state 
231 
>2 were selected for fragmentation using HCD with 28% normalized collision energy, dynamic 
232 
exclusion time of 25 s and profiler mode with positive polarity.  Alternatively, B31-Biotin labelled 
233 
peptides were analyzed using Agilent 1100 nano pump coupled to an LTQ Velos Pro-Orbitrap Elite 
234 
mass spectrometry (Thermo Scientific, USA).  Sample was loaded onto a trap column consisting of 
235 
a fritted capillary (360 μm o.d., 150 μm i.d.).  Peptides were separated with in-house packed column 
236 
with a 20 cm bed of C18 (Dr. Maisch ReproSil-Pur C18-AQ, 120 Å, 3 μm) having an integrated fritted 
237 
tip (360 μm o.d.), 75 μm i.d., 15 μm i.d. tip; New Objective).  Data-dependent acquisition was 
238 
performed by selecting top precursor ions for fragmentation using collision-induced dissociation 
239 
(CID) with 30 sec dynamic exclusion time limit.   
240 
 
Orbitrap Fusion Lumos 
241 
B31, B31-5A4, and MM1 pooled fractions – 14 fractions per isolate – were analyzed on a Vanquish 
242 
Neo UHPLC coupled to an Orbitrap Fusion Lumos instrument (Thermo Scientific, USA), equipped 
243 
with a Easy-Spray nanoelectrospray source.  Peptides were loaded onto a trap column (0.5 cm × 
244 
300-μm i.d., stationary phase C18) with a flow rate of 10 µL/min of mobile phase: 98% (vol/vol) LC-
245 
MS solvent A [0.1% (vol/vol) formic acid (FA) in water] and 2% (vol/vol) LC-MS solvent B [0.1% 
246 
(vol/vol) FA in acetonitrile].  Peptides were chromatographically separated on a 50-cm analytical 
247 
column [(EASY-Spray ES803A, Thermo Scientific); 75 µm × 50 cm, PepMap RSLC C18, 2-µm i.d, 100-
248 
Å-pore-size particles] applying a 115-min linear gradient: from 3% solvent B to 8% solvent B in 10 
249 
min, to 30% solvent B in 90 min, and ramped to 80% solvent B in 5 min, at a flow rate of 250 nL/min.  
250 
The column temperature was set to 45 °C.  Spray voltage was set to 1.8 kV and s-lens RF levels at 
251 
30%.  The mass spectrometer was set to high resolution data-dependent acquisition (DDA) of 15 
252

topN most intense ions with charge state of +2 to +5.  Each MS1 scan (120,000 resolving power at 
253 
200 m/z, automated gain control (AGC) of 125%, scan range 300 to 1,500 m/z, and dynamic 
254

255 
power at 200 m/z, AGC of 200%, maximum fill time of 54 ms).  Higher-energy collisional dissociation 
256 
(HCD) was used with 1.6 m/z isolation window and normalized collision energy of 30%.

Tims-TOF PRO 
275 
All 14 MM1 pooled fractions from high pH fractionation were spiked in with iRT standard peptides 
276 
(Biognosys AG, Schlieren, Switzerland) and subjected to mass spectrometry (MS) analysis using a 
277 
timsTOF PRO mass spectrometer (Bruker), coupled to a Vanquish Neo HPLC system (Thermo-Fisher 
278 
Scientific) in nanoflow setup for both Data-Dependent Acquisition-Parallel Accumulation-Serial 
279

Usage Notes 
574 
The Borrelia PeptideAtlas provides a publicly accessible resource, important for the Lyme disease 
575 
research community.  Our goal is to provide an expandable data source for many other B. 
576 
burgdorferi isolates, including clinically relevant isolates, and subjected to different growth 
577 
conditions, enabling the investigation of the dynamic proteome of this spirochete through its 
578 
infection stages and their vastly different environments.  The diverse proteomic information from 
579 
multiple infective isolates with credible data presented by the Borrelia PeptideAtlas can be useful 
580 
to pinpoint potential protein targets which are common to infective isolates and may be key in the 
581 
infection process – such as outer membrane proteins.  A list of membrane protein targets present 
582 
in the build can be identified. With in silico prediction of signal peptides and secondary structures 
583 
of membrane proteins, this dense proteomic data can be further investigated for host-pathogen 
584 
protein interactomics with different technologies.  Moreover, this resource provides access to 
585 
information regarding a wide range of potential proteins and PTMs relevant to chronic, acute and 
586 
post treatment Lyme disease to develop sensitive diagnostic assays in the Lyme community.  The 
587 
Borrelia PeptideAtlas is a dynamic proteome resource in terms of size and complexity and will be 
588 
updated to include new data periodically as more genomic and proteomic data is made available 
589 
for new clinical and laboratory isolates.  The collection of the raw data, protein, and peptide
